newsitem.title: USA: CBOT upbeat on yield-spread derivatives launch.
newsitem.headline: CBOT upbeat on yield-spread derivatives launch.

text.p: The Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) officials said they expect their new futures and options contracts on U.S. Treasury yield spreads to attract good demand when they are launched Friday.
"This is a simpler, easier-to-understand approach to hedging yield-curve risks," CBOT chairman Patrick Arbor said in a teleconference.
The launch date, just ahead of the U.S. presidential election and the Treasury's quarterly refunding in early November, should provide good hedging interest in intial trading, CBOT officials noted.
The Treasury in November will hold auctions for all maturity points covered by the new contracts, they said.
There will be contracts for any combination of two-, three-, five-, 10- and 30-year points on the curve, based on the most actively traded -- or "on-the-run" -- issues.
Both futures and options on futures will be cash-settled, meaning there will be no physical deliveries.

The fact that they will be based on on-the-run issues should attract new customer base and avoid taking business away from CBOT's existing T-bond and T-note futures, which are based on cheapest-to-deliver securities, the officials added.
"The differences are distinctive enough that we do not anticipate any cannibalization," said Eileen Klecka, senior marketing manager for CBOT.

Besides primary dealers, who must bid at every Treasury auction and have constant hedging needs, investors can use the contracts to change the duration of their portfolios in order to hedge risks or participate in a market movement, she said.
A longer duration portfolio is more sensitive to interest rate swings than shorter duration ones.
For local traders in the pit, the contracts will provide new arbitrage opportunities, CBOT officials added.
The officials boasted that the contracts had less risk than spread trading in cash Treasuries or OTC derivatives.

"The other side of the risk of a spread transaction (in cash Treasuries) is getting both sides of the trade done at the price that you need," said Jim Crystal, CBOT director of financial market products. "That risk goes away when you can execute a spread with one trade."
Margin requirements and clearing house functions, which would cut counterparty credit risk, should also help avoid disasters, the officials said.
Arbor said the yield-spread options offered a completely new trading vehicle.
"They are the world's only options on yield spreads, which make payoff profile much different from any other instrument," he said.
